new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for U has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements. Svantesson adds the first statement: U is tonal (four tones on major syllables) and the minor syllable of a sesquisyllable is unstressed, so prominence falls on the final/major syllable. Nothing in the catalog is contradicted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: U (Pa Xep variety) is a tone language: every major syllable carries one of four contrasting tones (high level, low level, falling, rising). Words are mono- or sesquisyllabic; in a sesquisyllable the minor (first) syllable is unstressed and the major (final) syllable is the stressed, tone-bearing one, i.e. the usual Mon-Khmer final-prominence pattern. There is no separate stress or accent section and no statement about stress in compounds or true polysyllables; 'unstressed position' on p. 74 refers to phrase-level reduction of whole words, not to a word-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. For tone: syllables with a stop coda (and, with few exceptions, coda -f) cannot have the falling tone; the rising tone is rare in open and sonorant-final syllables; low tone is often accompanied by creak or a final glottal stop (p. 74). Minor-syllable vowel is probably non-phonemic and reduces to schwa in running speech (p. 74-75). Expressives (rich in polysyllables in other Austroasiatic languages) were not investigated (p. 68).
new_statements.identity_note: Svantesson 1988 describes the U of Pǎ Xēp village (Shuangjiang area, Yunnan, China) as its main subject and proposes 'U' as a cover name for the closely related Pa Xep U, Pengpan U, Pangpin U, Pou Ma and Davies' P'u-man (pp. 64, 76-77). The tone description (four tones) is explicitly for Pa Xep U; Pengpan U and Pangpin U are said to share a complex tone system, while whether Pou Ma and P'u-man had tones cannot be determined (p. 77). Glottolog uuuu1243 = ISO 639-3 uuu 'U'

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages (p.68 secs 2.1/2.2; p.74 sec 2.2.3) are verbatim in the page scan we hold of Svantesson 1988, and the PDF's pp.64-66 confirm the languoid is Pa Xep U = Glottolog uuuu1243. (2) Deciding source is a 1988 70-page phonology-centred grammar sketch by a phonetician with instrumental tone verification; Glottolog lists it as the only description of U, and Hsiu's 2017 Angkuic survey (downloaded, open) confirms all Angkuic languages are tonal and that no fuller grammar/phonology of U exists. (3) list of works to obtain is two low-priority items (Svantesson 1989 Phonetica tonogenesis article, paywalled; Yan & Zhou 2012 Chinese survey, print) -- neither is expected to alter a tonal / sesquisyllabic-iambic-by-word-shape coding.
